anchorData: All figures are illustrative (made-up) but realistic. SURVEYOR: Wanjiru Kamau, Nairobi. Her clinometer reads the angle of elevation of the top of a tall office building as 35 degrees. She stands 100 m from the foot of the building on level ground (distance measured with a tape or trundle wheel along the ground). Her eye height is 1.5 m. Height of the building above eye level = 100 x tan 35 degrees = 100 x 0.7002 = 70.02 m, which is 70.0 m to 1 d.p. Total building height = 70.0 + 1.5 = 71.5 m. SCHOOL FLAGPOLE (same angle, small triangle): at a set time the Sun's angle of elevation is 35 degrees and the flagpole's shadow on level ground is 8.0 m long. Height = 8.0 x 0.7002 = 5.60 m, so 5.6 m. Check: 5.6 / 8.0 = 0.70 and 70.0 / 100 = 0.70. Both triangles have the same ratio opposite/adjacent (about 0.70) because both have a 35 degree angle. This is the puzzle. DRAWN TRIANGLES FOR LESSON 2 (all right-angled, acute angle 35 degrees, lengths in cm to the nearest mm): Triangle A: adjacent 4.0, opposite 2.8, hypotenuse 4.9. Triangle B: adjacent 8.0, opposite 5.6, hypotenuse 9.8. Triangle C: adjacent 12.0, opposite 8.4, hypotenuse 14.6. Measured ratios: opp/adj = 0.70 in all three; opp/hyp = 0.571, 0.571, 0.575 (about 0.57); adj/hyp = 0.816, 0.816, 0.822 (about 0.82). Small differences are measurement error. TABLE VALUES (4 d.p., from tables or calculator): angle: sin, cos, tan. 10: 0.1736, 0.9848, 0.1763. 20: 0.3420, 0.9397, 0.3640. 30: 0.5000, 0.8660, 0.5774. 35: 0.5736, 0.8192, 0.7002. 40: 0.6428, 0.7660, 0.8391. 45: 0.7071, 0.7071, 1.0000. 50: 0.7660, 0.6428, 1.1918. 55: 0.8192, 0.5736, 1.4281. 60: 0.8660, 0.5000, 1.7321. 70: 0.9397, 0.3420, 2.7475. 80: 0.9848, 0.1736, 5.6713. 90: sin 1, cos 0, tan undefined. Complement pairs used in Lesson 4: 10/80, 20/70, 30/60, 35/55, 40/50, 45/45. Example: sin 35 = 0.5736 = cos 55; cos 35 = 0.8192 = sin 55. Lesson 5 check: sin 35 / cos 35 = 0.5736 / 0.8192 = 0.7002 = tan 35. SPECIAL ANGLES (exact): isosceles right triangle with equal sides 1 and hypotenuse root 2: sin 45 = 1/root2 = 0.7071, cos 45 = 1/root2, tan 45 = 1. Equilateral triangle of side 2 cut in half gives a right triangle with sides 1, root3, 2 (angles 30, 60, 90): sin 30 = 1/2, cos 30 = root3/2 = 0.8660, tan 30 = 1/root3 = 0.5774; sin 60 = root3/2, cos 60 = 1/2, tan 60 = root3 = 1.7321. Table for 90 degrees: sin 90 = 1, cos 90 = 0, tan 90 undefined (simplification: the triangle degenerates). LADDER EXAMPLE (Lesson 1 sides and Lesson 6 or 8 check): a 4.0 m ladder leans on a wall making 60 degrees with the ground: height reached = 4.0 x sin 60 = 3.46 m (3.5 m to 1 d.p.), foot of ladder from wall = 4.0 x cos 60 = 2.0 m. LESSON 7 CLINOMETER SET: (a) the school flagpole viewed from 10.0 m with clinometer reading 30 degrees and eye height 1.5 m: height above eye = 10.0 x 0.5774 = 5.77 m, total = 7.27 m, about 7.3 m (illustrative; note this is a worked example, learners take their own readings for their real measurements). (b) angle of depression: a person on a balcony 70.0 m above the ground sees a parked matatu at angle of depression 35 degrees; horizontal distance = 70.0 / 0.7002 = 99.97 m, about 100 m. (c) a 60 degree check: a tower viewed from 30.0 m with elevation 60 degrees: height above eye = 30.0 x 1.7321 = 51.96 m, about 52.0 m; add 1.5 m eye height = 53.5 m.
characters: Wanjiru Kamau: surveyor in Nairobi; clinometer eye height 1.5 m; stands 100 m from the building; reads 35 degrees; building 71.5 m tall in total (70.0 m above eye level). The tall office building: fictional, in Nairobi CBD, on level ground. Mwangaza Secondary School: fictional school where learners work; has a flagpole whose shadow is 8.0 m when the Sun's elevation is 35 degrees, height 5.6 m. Teacher: Mr Otieno, fictional Mathematics teacher who asks the driving question. Learners work in groups of 4 or 5 and keep a class Driving Question Board (DQB) and a class model (a poster of 'angle -> ratio of sides -> unknown length'). Ladder: 4.0 m ladder on a wall at 60 degrees. Matatu: parked on the road below a 70.0 m balcony, 100 m away horizontally (Lesson 7). Only these people, places and figures may be used for the shared story; writers may add small extra everyday objects (roof, ramp, ladder) but must not give them new numbers that conflict with this sheet.
outcome: Wanjiru measures 100 m along level ground from the foot of the building and reads a 35 degree angle of elevation. Because every right-angled triangle with a 35 degree angle has the same ratio opposite/adjacent (tan 35 = 0.7002, about 0.70), whether it is the 8.0 m shadow triangle of the flagpole or the 100 m triangle of the building, she multiplies 100 x 0.7002 = 70.0 m and adds her eye height of 1.5 m to state a height of 71.5 m without climbing. The angle fixes the shape of the triangle, so it fixes the ratios of the sides, and the ratios (sine, cosine, tangent) link a known side to an unknown side.
conventions: Right-angled triangle: the hypotenuse is the side opposite the right angle (longest). For a chosen acute angle (called theta, written as the Greek letter theta or as the angle in degrees), opposite is the side facing it and adjacent is the side next to it that is not the hypotenuse. Definitions used by every lesson: sin theta = opposite / hypotenuse; cos theta = adjacent / hypotenuse; tan theta = opposite / adjacent. Short forms: sin, cos, tan. Angles are in degrees and calculators must be in DEG mode. Table and calculator values are written to 4 decimal places; lengths in answers are given to 1 d.p. or 2 d.p. as stated. Complementary angles: two acute angles that add up to 90 degrees. Use the phrase 'sine of an angle equals cosine of its complement' i.e. sin theta = cos(90 - theta). tan theta = sin theta / cos theta. Angle of elevation: the angle above the horizontal from the observer's eye up to the object. Angle of depression: the angle below the horizontal from the observer's eye down to the object (equal to the angle of elevation from the object to the observer, alternate angles). Height of an object found with a clinometer = (horizontal distance x tan of angle) + eye height. Say 'trigonometric ratios' not 'trig formulas'. Use the word 'ratio' for the quotient of two sides. Tables mean four-figure mathematical tables. Kenyan contexts only: ugali, maize and similar food examples may appear for ratio or scale analogies, places such as Nairobi, Kisumu, Rift Valley. Exact special-angle values use root2 and root3 with decimals in brackets. Do not teach the sine rule, cosine rule or angles larger than 90 degrees, which are outside this sub-strand. Learning outcomes covered across lessons: (a) determine the trigonometric ratios of acute angles from mathematical tables and calculators, (b) relate sines and cosines of complementary angles, (c) relate the sine, cosine and tangent of acute angles, (d) determine the trigonometric ratios of special angles 30, 45, 60 and 90 using triangles, (e) apply trigonometric ratios to angles of elevation and depression, (f) reflect on the use of trigonometry in real-life situations. KICD key inquiry questions to copy verbatim: What is trigonometry? How do we use trigonometry in real-life situations? Lessons last 40 minutes unless stated; phase minutes must sum to 40.

lessonMap.focus: Right-angled triangles around us and the surveyor puzzle
lessonMap.teaches: Identify right-angled triangles in the school environment, draw them, and name the hypotenuse, opposite and adjacent sides relative to a marked acute angle; launch the DQB and first model.
lessonMap.buildsOn: No earlier lesson; builds on Grade 9 knowledge of triangles and the Pythagorean theorem.
lessonMap.usesData: Surveyor Wanjiru Kamau (35 degree reading, 100 m) and the flagpole shadow (8.0 m, 35 degrees) shown as the puzzle only; the 4.0 m ladder at 60 degrees for naming sides. No ratio values yet.

lessonMap.focus: Same angle, same ratio: defining sine, cosine, tangent
lessonMap.teaches: Measure sides of right-angled triangles with the same acute angle but different sizes, see that opp/adj, opp/hyp and adj/hyp are constant, and define sin, cos and tan.
lessonMap.buildsOn: Lesson 1: naming hypotenuse, opposite and adjacent; the puzzle of the flagpole and the building.
lessonMap.usesData: Drawn triangles A, B and C with a 35 degree angle and their measured ratios; the link 5.6/8.0 = 70.0/100 = 0.70.

lessonMap.focus: Getting ratios from tables and calculators
lessonMap.teaches: Read sin, cos and tan of acute angles from four-figure tables and a scientific calculator in DEG mode, and check them against the ratios measured in Lesson 2.
lessonMap.buildsOn: Lesson 2: the definitions of sin, cos, tan and the measured values for 35 degrees.
lessonMap.usesData: The 4 d.p. table values for 35 degrees (0.5736, 0.8192, 0.7002) compared with triangles A, B, C; further angles 10, 20, 40, 50, 70, 80.

lessonMap.focus: Complementary angles: sin theta = cos(90 - theta)
lessonMap.teaches: Generate a table of angles and their complements, and establish that the sine of an angle equals the cosine of its complement (and cos equals sin of the complement).
lessonMap.buildsOn: Lesson 3: reading values from tables and calculators; Lesson 2: the definitions (opposite and adjacent swap when the other acute angle is used).

lessonMap.focus: tan theta = sin theta / cos theta and how ratios change
lessonMap.teaches: Use the table of values to establish tan theta = sin theta / cos theta, and describe how sin, cos and tan change as the acute angle increases from 10 to 80 degrees.
lessonMap.buildsOn: Lessons 2 and 3: definitions and tabulated values; Lesson 4: the table of values already generated.
lessonMap.usesData: Check sin 35 / cos 35 = 0.5736 / 0.8192 = 0.7002 = tan 35; the trends in the 10 to 80 degree table; tan 35 = 0.7002 as the surveyor's multiplier.

lessonMap.teaches: Derive the exact ratios of 45 degrees from an isosceles right-angled triangle and of 30 and 60 degrees from half an equilateral triangle, and complete the special-angle table including 90 degrees.
lessonMap.buildsOn: Lesson 2: definitions; Lesson 4: complements (sin 30 = cos 60); Lesson 5: tan = sin/cos used to check; Lesson 3: decimal values to check.
lessonMap.usesData: Special angles data: triangle with sides 1, 1, root2; triangle with sides 1, root3, 2; exact and decimal values; 4.0 m ladder at 60 degrees.

lessonMap.focus: Clinometer, angles of elevation and depression
lessonMap.teaches: Build and use a simple clinometer (protractor, string, weight, straw), define angles of elevation and depression, and calculate heights and distances using height = distance x tan angle + eye height.
lessonMap.buildsOn: Lessons 2, 3 and 5: tan as opposite/adjacent from tables or calculator; Lesson 6: special-angle values for exact checks; Lesson 1: the surveyor's instrument.
lessonMap.usesData: Worked examples: flagpole from 10.0 m at 30 degrees (7.3 m total), balcony 70.0 m and matatu at 35 degrees depression (about 100 m), tower at 60 degrees from 30.0 m (53.5 m); learners also take their own real readings.

lessonMap.focus: Back to the surveyor: final explanation and reflection
lessonMap.teaches: Apply the ratios to solve the full surveyor problem (and a related ladder or depression problem) and explain why the same angle gives the same ratio for small and large triangles; revise the class model and DQB; reflect on the use of trigonometry in real-life situations.
lessonMap.buildsOn: Lessons 1 to 7: sides and naming (1), constant ratios and definitions (2), tables and calculator (3), complements (4), tan = sin/cos and trends (5), special angles (6), clinometer, elevation and depression (7).
lessonMap.usesData: The full anchorData: Wanjiru at 100 m, 35 degrees, eye height 1.5 m, building 71.5 m; flagpole shadow 8.0 m, height 5.6 m; ladder 4.0 m at 60 degrees; balcony and matatu example.
